job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Bianca Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings I help my mum in the family dental practice, answering the phone and booking patients, three days a week, mostly so I'm not alone with my laptop. Then I do job applications from about eleven until the afternoon. I've sent 35 applications since the summer, had six interviews, and lost one final round in September to someone who already worked at the bank.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Economics and finance at the university in Corley, a good result. I spent ten weeks in loan operations at a regional bank, checking mortgage paperwork. I use AI now and then, mainly to tidy my cover letters, but I always rewrite what it gives me because it sounds like everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a relief, but not a victory. At the dinner table I'd tell my dad that a lot of the fuss was companies hoping to cut staff and call it progress. Online I'd stay out of it, though I'd probably share an article about workers' rights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my search is still hard for the old reasons: too many graduates, too few junior posts, and everyone wanting experience. Small automations still chip at loan paperwork, which is what I did at the bank. So even a quiet world has pressure on my first job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, about eight a week, and ask my internship manager Mr Kaplan for a reference and for any contacts. I'd take a short bookkeeping certificate to widen my options. And I'd keep helping my mum at the practice for pocket money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, a bit uneasy. I'm not scared, but I'm waiting for something to happen, and waiting is draining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a first job change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would a first job change for you?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does helping at the practice sit with the job hunt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot. I'd move out of Corley to share a flat with my friend Anjali, pay my own bills and stop being the person who still sleeps in her childhood bedroom. Having a payslip would feel like someone finally agreeing I'm an adult.

say: I'd say it's a **relief** but not a victory, as much of the fuss was firms hoping to cut staff.
I'd share articles on workers' rights online.
think: My search stays hard for old reasons: too many graduates, too few **junior posts**.
Small automations still chip away at loan paperwork, my internship work.
do: Send about **eight applications** a week and ask Mr Kaplan for a reference.
Keep helping at my mum's dental practice for pocket money.
feel: Slightly **uneasy**: not scared, but waiting is draining.
S0.quote: Having a payslip would feel like someone finally agreeing I'm an adult.
fieldNote: Sees the problem as **too many graduates**, not as technology, in the quiet world.
Her plan is practical: references, a short certificate and steady applications.
The wish to move out gives the job hunt emotional weight.

steps.text: Send eight job applications a week
Ask Mr Kaplan for a reference and bank contacts
Take a short bookkeeping certificate in the evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where it gets serious. Most of what a junior does, the checking and the paperwork, is the first thing software takes. I'd tell friends to learn the tools but also to demand that firms keep hiring trainees, and I'd sign any petition that says so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my pathway shrinks. Loan operations at the bank had twelve juniors on my floor, and I can easily see it becoming five. But I also think there are new roles checking what the software does, and I'd be good at that if I got in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI tools properly instead of casually, and take an online course in data analysis through the university. I'd apply to the bank's risk and compliance teams, not just operations. And I'd ask my uncle Raj, who works in insurance, whether he could connect me with his manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. A bit anxious about the first job, but I feel more in control than I do right now, because there's something to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use AI properly. What's different from how you use it now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you'd use AI properly. What's different from how you use it now?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should step in to keep trainee jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I use it like a spellchecker. Then I'd use it to build a model of a loan portfolio and explain what it shows, which is a skill an employer can see. I'd put a project like that on my CV, with real numbers, so nobody has to guess what I can do.

say: I'd say this is where it gets serious, and firms must keep **hiring trainees**.
I'd tell friends to learn the tools and sign petitions.
think: My bank floor had **twelve juniors** and could easily have five.
New roles checking what software does could suit me if I get in.
do: Learn AI tools **properly** and take an online data analysis course.
Apply to **risk and compliance** teams, not only operations.
Ask my uncle Raj, who works in insurance, for an introduction.
feel: **Mixed**: anxious about the first job but more in control, with something to learn.
S1.quote: I'd put a project like that on my CV, with real numbers, so nobody has to guess what I can do.
fieldNote: Moves from casual to **deliberate** AI use once the threat is believable.
Uses personal contacts, her uncle Raj, as a real route into work.
Keeps her progressive stance: wants rules that protect trainees.

steps.text: Build a loan portfolio model with AI tools for my CV
Apply to bank risk and compliance teams
Finish an online data analysis course through the university
Sign petitions asking firms to keep trainee schemes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments have to act now, because two years is not enough time for schools, firms or families. I'd back a shorter working week and some kind of basic income, and I'd say so loudly. At the practice I'd tell my mum we should look at how patients book, because that part is easy to automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a lot of what I trained for goes before I've even finished my first contract. Banks would hire a handful of experts and let software do the rest. I'd be one of thousands with the same degree, and the family cushion would stop looking so generous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop waiting for the perfect finance job. I'd apply for anything with people in it, such as client service, hospital administration or the council, and I'd put my savings into a three-month course in project management. I'd also talk with my parents about whether I should stay home longer instead of renting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, in a quiet way. I'd be doing the sums at night and then telling everyone at breakfast that I was fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your brother Dev, who's in secondary school?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you tell your brother Dev, who's in secondary school?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents about staying home longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my brother Dev not to follow me into finance just because it looked safe. I'd tell him to find something where he works with people and makes decisions, and to learn how the machines work whatever he picks. I'd not want him to blame himself later for a world he didn't choose.

say: I'd say governments must act now and back a **shorter week** and basic income.
I'd warn my mum that patient booking at the practice is easy to automate.
think: Much of what I trained for could go before my first contract, leaving **thousands** with my degree.
The family cushion would stop looking so generous.
do: Apply for roles with people in them: client service, hospital **administration**, the council.
Put savings into a three-month **project management** course.
Talk with my parents about staying home longer.
feel: **Scared** in a quiet way, doing sums at night and saying I'm fine at breakfast.
S2.quote: I'd tell my brother Dev not to follow me into finance just because it looked safe.
fieldNote: Her **public confidence** hides private sums, a gap she names herself.
Shifts from finance-specific jobs to anything involving people.
Protective of her younger brother, showing the stakes at home.

steps.text: Apply for client service and hospital administration jobs
Spend savings on a three-month project management course
Back a shorter working week in a local campaign
Stay at home longer instead of renting a flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a window and we shouldn't waste it. I'd say firms should start training schemes now and governments should write the rules while people still have jobs. To friends I'd say pick a path that mixes numbers and people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm okay if I act. If I get a job in the next year, I'd have time to move into something like risk or advisory, which needs a person to answer for the decision. But I know some people won't be okay, and a few of my friends are sitting still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any decent graduate offer by spring, then start the professional exam for risk analysts. I'd move into a flat share with Anjali after my first six months of pay. And I'd put at least a fifth of my salary into a savings account, since I don't know what year five looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier. Five years sounds frightening and workable at the same time, like a deadline you can plan towards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would a person still be needed in risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why would a person still be needed in risk?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which friends are sitting still, and what would you say to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because somebody has to be named when things go wrong. Regulators and boards won't accept the software did it, so they'll want a person who signs. That's what I'm trying to become, the one who signs.

say: I'd say five years is a **window** and firms should start training schemes now.
I'd advise friends to pick a path mixing numbers and people.
think: If I get a job within the year, I'd have time to move into **risk** or advisory.
Some of my friends are sitting still, and I worry about them.
do: Take a decent graduate offer by **spring** and begin a risk analyst exam.
Share a flat with Anjali after six months of pay.
Save at least **a fifth** of my salary.
feel: **Steadier**: frightening and workable at once, a deadline to plan towards.
S3.quote: Regulators and boards won't accept the software did it, so they'll want a person who signs.
fieldNote: Has a clear theory of where human roles survive: **accountability**.
The flat share with Anjali is a milestone she keeps returning to.
Worried about friends who are not acting, a social anxiety.

steps.text: Accept a graduate offer by spring
Start the professional risk analyst exams
Save a fifth of every salary
Move into a flat share with Anjali

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to build a decent safety net if people use it well. I'd back retraining funded by firms and public pensions that don't depend on one job. I'd also tell friends it's okay to be hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd manage. I'd have time to get a first job, move to a second, and become the person who understands the software and the clients. I'd worry more for people in their fifties who haven't got that time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a job this winter, take a part-time master's in data and finance over three years, and keep saving. I'd also look at volunteering with a credit union, where the work is about people and money together. I'd keep helping my mum when I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, actually. Ten years feels like a long road, and I can see myself walking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in the long timeline that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Is there anything in the long timeline that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why credit union work in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People will assume nothing will change and put it off. I might do that myself. Ten years of being comfortable is its own risk, because the day it arrives you're 33 and nothing is ready.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to build a **safety net** if people use it well.
I'd back firm-funded retraining and pensions that don't hang on one job.
think: I think I'd **manage**: first job, second job, then the person who understands software and clients.
I worry more about people in their fifties.
do: Get a job this winter and take a part-time **master's** in data and finance.
Volunteer with a **credit union**, where work mixes people and money.
Keep saving and helping my mum.
feel: Fairly **calm**: a long road I can see myself walking.
S4.quote: Ten years of being comfortable is its own risk, because the day it arrives you're 33 and nothing is ready.
fieldNote: Reasonably secure, yet notices that **comfort** may delay action.
Her concern reaches beyond herself to older workers.
Plans stack neatly: job, master's, savings and volunteering.

steps.text: Take a graduate job by this winter
Study a part-time master's in data and finance
Volunteer at a credit union on Saturdays

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, because everything depends on whether I get a first job before the entry roles vanish. What would help is a graduate scheme guaranteed by law, clear rules on telling people when software makes a decision about them, and a bit of money for retraining.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm lucky, and I know it. A strong cushion and a supportive family buy me time, and plenty of people my age don't have either. I'd want any plan to cover them.

headlineQuote: A strong cushion and a supportive family buy me time, and plenty of people my age don't have either.
portrait: Bianca is 23, a finance graduate living at home in Corley, **35 applications** in and six interviews done.
She uses AI tools occasionally and moves to **serious use** once the threat is believable.
Her progressive views make her want rules, trainee schemes and shorter weeks, and she signs petitions.
She keeps a public air of confidence while doing worried sums at night.
Her theory is that people who **sign for decisions** will still be needed, and she aims to become one.
biggestWorry: The **AGI by 2028** picture worries her most, since the first job must land before entry roles vanish.
whatWouldHelp: A graduate scheme backed by **law** and clear rules on telling people when software decides about them.
A bit of money for retraining, extended to people without family cushions.
